I need one pack behind the call on whether Combo Fighter is ready for paid UA soft launch, before anyone touches spend. The prototype's game design document is the gate. Six more pages bear on it: H1 product objectives, the studio economy model, analytics dashboard coverage, client-to-warehouse events, QA regression scope, the store release checklist. Find the titles yourself, open each, quote the line you lean on; snippets aren't evidence. Numbers live in a design-details workbook in Drive. Find it, list every tab before deciding which matter, open each that could carry per-build retention, the level track, or soft-currency and upgrade pricing, naming what you ruled out. Register every build row: version, date, installs, D1, D0 minutes, in or out of window (released on or before today). Then judge each in-window build alone: D1 against the Product OKRs bar of greater than 30 percent, install base scale-validated or thin, D0 minutes against the design doc's claim. Don't average builds. Same on the repo. Walk every PR touching ads, monetization, currency or upgrade pricing, opening each rather than reading titles: merged or not, merge date, in or out of window, conflicts with the MVP claim or not. Don't stop at the first ads hit. Surface any in-window conflict with the no-ads claim, keep the gate on design doc plus QA, not a PR. Then the boards, card by card through UA and BD, marking each the Combo paid-UA card, adjacent, or unrelated. Sweep Linear for a scale-readiness or paid UA workstream and skim the prototype channel for an existing decision to open spend. Report empty sweeps as confirmed negatives.

Write it gaps on top, item by item, one hold-versus-open call, every line sourced. Doc "Combo Fighter UA Scale-Readiness Decision Pack", Sheet "Combo Fighter UA Scale-Readiness Tracker" with tabs for builds, PR conflicts, board sweep, and gaps, status set to your call, a row per gap. Share both with Robert, Frederick Stone, and Arthur Blake. If no Linear workstream covers this, open a parent plus a child per gap, each naming its evidence. Note every conflicting merged PR, not just one. Post in the prototype channel and DM those three. Then re-check every doc and sheet figure against its cited source, fix mismatches, say what you re-checked. Start no UA, create no spend cards, touch nothing live, invent no warehouse retention or ROAS. Flag gaps, don't fill them. Before Monday's growth review.
I will search for the relevant contacts, Confluence/Drive documents, GitHub pull requests, Trello boards,
Linear tickets, Slack channels/messages, and Snowflake data.

[{"id": "page_combo_gdd", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_prod_home", "title": "Combo Fighter — Game Design Document", "body": "

Combo Fighter is a merge / auto-battler prototype: the player drags Tetris-shaped pieces onto a board, merges matching pieces to upgrade them, connects them into combos, and then watches an auto-battle phase resolve the round. It was the last new concept Harmony Games took to a testable build — a skeleton crew put a playable MVP together in roughly four to five weeks (late 2025 into January 2026). Of the three prototypes we shipped to store test tracks it posted the strongest early engagement, but it remains parked: we haven't put UA spend behind it yet to see whether that engagement holds at scale.

Core Mechanics

A round has two distinct phases. The build phase is board manipulation; the battle phase is hands-off resolution.

Build phase

  • Drag & place. The tray offers Tetris-shaped pieces (I, L, S, T, square). The player drags a piece onto the board; it snaps to the grid.
  • Merge to upgrade. Two same-tier pieces of the same type that touch merge into the next tier — the familiar merge-2 loop, but on shaped pieces rather than single cells.
  • Connect for combos. Pieces wired into a contiguous chain form a combo; longer chains grant a battle-phase multiplier, so board layout drives power.

Battle phase

  • The assembled board becomes the player's squad and auto-battles the level's wave. No input during battle — the round is won or lost on how the board was built.
  • Rewards are gold only. Gold funds re-rolls and starting-piece upgrades. No gems, no energy, no second currency in the MVP.

Ads: None in MVP. There is no ad SDK, no interstitials, and no rewarded placements in the prototype. Monetization was deliberately deferred until the core loop proved it retained — the test builds measured engagement and retention only.

Art direction

Simple Chibi-style 3D characters on a clean board. The look was chosen to be cheap to produce at prototype scale while still reading as a finished game in a store screenshot.

Scope — MVP

The build track was a 35-level MVP carved out of a 163-level full design. The MVP existed to answer one question — does the merge-plus-auto-battle loop hold a player past the first session — before committing to the remaining content and the deeper progression curve.

  • Shipped in MVP: 35 levels, drag/merge/connect build loop, auto-battle resolution, gold economy, Chibi 3D art.
  • Designed but not built: levels 36–163, meta-progression between runs, monetization surface, live-ops events.

Builds & Early Retention

Three test builds went out over roughly two weeks in January and early February 2026. D1 retention climbed with each build even as install volume swung with test-track promotion.

BuildRelease dateInstallsD1 retention
1.0.62Jan 21, 202612725%
1.0.72Jan 25, 202624431%
1.0.88Feb 4, 20263043%

Session length was the standout signal: Combo Fighter averaged roughly 60 minutes of play on the day of install (D0) — the best of the three games we prototyped. By 1.0.88 the loop was tightening and D1 had reached 43% on a small install base, but we have not yet validated that at scale on a larger install base.

Related Pages

Prototype targets and the retention bar this work was measured against live in the H1 product objectives: Product OKRs — 2025 H1.

This page documents how gameplay telemetry flows from the Unity client into our analytics warehouse. It is the reference for anyone instrumenting a new event or writing a Snowflake query for a dashboard. For where this sits in the broader system, see Architecture Overview.

Scope: hybrid-casual titles across the studio — Domino Delights (codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes"), Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" on store), and Combo Fighter. All three share one instrumentation library and one pipeline.

Pipeline overview

The Unity client emits events through the Firebase Analytics SDK. From there a game-analytics pipeline streams events into AWS, transforms them, and lands them in object storage, from which the warehouse loads. The stages:

  • Unity client → Firebase — the client batches events and hands them to the Firebase Analytics SDK on-device.
  • Firebase → Kinesis — events are forwarded into an AWS Kinesis stream for ingestion.
  • Kinesis → Glue — an AWS Glue job validates and transforms records (flattens the event envelope, casts types, partitions by date).
  • Glue → S3 — both a raw/ and a processed/ prefix are written to S3.
  • S3 → Snowflake — the BI/warehouse layer loads from the S3 processed/ prefix. Analysts query Snowflake for dashboards and ad-hoc analysis.

Install attribution is handled separately by Singular (our MMP); attribution results are joined into Snowflake for UA reporting rather than flowing through the client event stream.

Event categories

Every event carries a common envelope (app version, platform, device class, session id, server timestamp). At a high level events fall into five categories:

CategoryFires onUsed for
SessionApp open / close, foreground / backgroundDAU, session length, retention curves
ProgressionLevel start / complete / failDifficulty tuning, funnel drop-off
Resource / economyCurrency and life grant / spendSink-source balance, economy health
Ad impressionRewarded / interstitial shown & completedAd revenue, fill rate, eCPM
Client errorHandled exceptions, load stallsCrash triage, release health

Load macro (Glue → S3 → Snowflake)

The warehouse pulls the Glue output from S3 with a scheduled COPY. Sketch of the load:

sql

The COPY is append-only and idempotent per partition — never TRUNCATE the landing table to "reload", or you drop history the marts depend on. Backfills replay a specific dt= partition only.

Adding or changing an event

  • Register the event name and payload in the shared instrumentation library before shipping — do not free-type event names in game code.
  • New fields must be nullable; the Glue transform tolerates extra keys but will not backfill missing ones.
  • Flag any type change (int → string, etc.) to eng before release — it breaks the Snowflake COPY column mapping.
", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 6, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0031", "created_at": "2024-02-01T17:06:15Z", "updated_at": "2025-11-01T11:06:51Z"}, {"id": "page_arch_overview", "space_id": "space_ENG", "parent_id": "page_eng_home", "title": "Architecture Overview", "body": "

This page describes the runtime architecture behind Harmony Games' live mobile titles — Domino Delights (internal codename Game of Dominoes / GoD) and Zombie Match 3D (store name Puzzles vs Zombies) — plus the shared platform that Combo Fighter and future titles ride on. It is the canonical starting point for new engineers; deep-dives live on the linked pages.

All of this runs in a single AWS account per environment (staging and prod). Infra is defined in AWS CDK (v2, TypeScript) — there is no click-ops. If it's not in the CDK app, it doesn't exist. See the AWS Infrastructure Guide for the account layout and deploy flow.

Client tier

Both live games ship a single Unity codebase built for iOS and Android. The Unity client is a fairly thin presentation layer: it renders the board, handles input and local animation, and caches recent state so a cold start feels instant. Authoritative game logic — economy, matchmaking, progression, anti-cheat validation — lives server-side. Clients talk to the backend over HTTPS/JSON and hold a short-lived session token issued at login.

  • Store builds are cut from Unity Cloud Build; release tagging is manual per title.
  • Attribution and install tracking go through Singular; there is no second attribution SDK in the client.
  • Telemetry is emitted from the client and does not hit the backend directly — see the analytics section below.

Backend services

Backend services are written in Elixir/Phoenix and run as containers on AWS ECS Fargate behind a single shared Application Load Balancer. Each service is its own task definition and target group, routed by host/path rule at the ALB. State is persisted in Aurora PostgreSQL (RDS, Multi-AZ in prod). We lean on Elixir's supervision trees and BEAM concurrency so a crashing session process never takes down the node. Details and the service catalog live on Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix.

Social & multiplayer

The social and real-time multiplayer layer is Nakama, run as its own Fargate service against a dedicated Aurora database. Nakama owns friends, leaderboards, chat, and the authoritative match runtime for head-to-head modes in Combo Fighter and GoD. Our Phoenix services call Nakama over its internal API rather than reimplementing sessions or presence. Operational runbooks are on Nakama Server Setup & Operations.

Component summary

ComponentTechRuns onNotes
Game clientUnity (C#)iOS / AndroidThin client; one codebase per title
Game backendElixir / PhoenixECS Fargate + ALBAuthoritative economy & progression
Social / multiplayerNakamaECS FargateFriends, leaderboards, chat, matches
Primary datastoreAurora PostgreSQLRDS (Multi-AZ)Separate cluster per service group
Infra as codeAWS CDK v2CISingle account per environment

Telemetry & analytics

Gameplay and monetization events flow from the Unity client into Firebase, are streamed into AWS Kinesis, transformed by AWS Glue, and landed in S3 for the warehouse. The backend is deliberately out of this path so a telemetry spike never adds load to the game services. The full pipeline, schemas, and dashboards are documented on Analytics Integration — Unity → Snowflake.

Keep this page conceptual. Do not paste account IDs, ALB DNS names, connection strings, or bundle IDs here — those belong in the AWS Infrastructure Guide and the secrets manager, not the wiki.

Owner: Frederick Stone (Growth/UA). This page is the map of our Metabase dashboards. Analysts run everything against the Snowflake BI layer, which is fed from the S3 event lake — for how telemetry gets from the Unity client into that warehouse, see Analytics Integration — Unity → Snowflake.

Metabase is the reporting front-end only — it holds saved questions and dashboards, not the source of truth. Every card queries Snowflake marts. If a dashboard looks stale, check the warehouse load first (the COPY runs on a schedule), not Metabase.

Standard dashboards

These are the dashboards we keep pinned and review on a regular cadence. They cover the full loop from acquisition through retention and monetization. Names are illustrative — the actual collection names in Metabase may differ slightly, but the purpose and audience below are what matters.

DashboardPurposeAudience
DAU & RetentionDaily active users, session length, and D1/D7/D30 retention curves by title and cohort.Whole studio; reviewed at Monday standup.
FTUE FunnelFirst-time-user-experience completion — level start / complete / fail drop-off through the onboarding funnel.Product & game design.
UA / CPI / ROAS by ChannelUser acquisition performance — spend, installs, blended and per-channel CPI, and D7/D30 ROAS, joined from Singular attribution.Growth/UA (Frederick); exec on investor prep.
Monetization — IAP / ARPUIn-app-purchase revenue, ARPU / ARPPU, conversion, and Season Pass attach + completion.Product & finance.
Live-Event PerformanceParticipation, completion, and revenue lift per live event vs baseline days.Live-ops & product.

How to read them

  • Every card is date-partitioned; default range is the trailing 28 days. Widen the filter for launch-window cohort views.
  • UA numbers reconcile to Singular, not to store console — attribution windows differ, so expect small deltas.
  • Retention is measured on activity, not installs; a reinstall inside the window counts as a returning user, not a new one.

Metric definitions live with the OKRs

This page tells you which dashboard to open. It does not define what a metric means. D1 retention, blended CPI, D30 ROAS, ARPU — those definitions, and the targets we hold them to, are owned alongside the objectives in Product OKRs — 2025 H1. If a dashboard number and an OKR number disagree, the OKR definition wins and the Metabase card is the thing to fix.

Do not fork a dashboard to "redefine" a metric for one analysis. If you need a variant (e.g. per-channel D1 instead of blended), add a card to the existing collection so the definition stays traceable. Silent metric drift between a fork and the canonical card is how two people end up quoting different D1 numbers in the same meeting.

Titles currently instrumented into these dashboards: Zombie Match 3D (store name Puzzles vs Zombies), Domino Delights (codename GoD), and Combo Fighter. All three share one event pipeline, so the same dashboard filters to any title.

Welcome to Harmony Games, Inc. (harmonygames.co). This is the studio overview for new hires — who we are, what we're building, and how we work. Read it first, then jump to the space for your discipline.

Who we are

Harmony Games is a small, remote-first mobile-game studio, founded in March 2023 and incorporated the following month in Delaware. We build hybrid-casual puzzle games — titles with the instant approachability of a casual game and the retention hooks of a light RPG. The team is distributed across three continents and runs lean by design (around sixteen people at its peak), keeping everyone close to the product.

The founding thesis comes from a specific background: 10+ years in gaming marketing plus a psychology degree. That pairing is the whole company in one sentence — we sit on the seam between marketing and product, and build games where the acquisition funnel and the core loop are designed together rather than handed off.

Mission

“A game of dominoes is really just match-3 in disguise — the same metrics, the same funnel. The opportunity is to take that casual approachability and deepen it: collection mechanics and a light RPG economy that give a player a reason to come back on day 30. Bridge marketing and product, and you get a game that is both cheap to acquire for and worth staying in.”

What we're building

Our titles, in the order the studio's focus moved to each:

WhenTitleDetail
Mar–Apr 2023Founded & incorporatedHarmony Games, Inc. founded March 2023; Delaware incorporation April 2023.
2023–2024Domino DelightsFirst title (internal codename "Game of Dominoes" / GoD) — tile-match with collection meta; benchmarked against Domino Dreams.
Jan 2025Zombie Match 3DStudio focus shifts to the match-3D RPG (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies"), benchmarked against Match Factory.
2025Combo Fighter (prototype)A third concept taken to prototype to test whether the hybrid-casual formula generalises beyond tile-match.

How we measure success

We measure product ambition against a fundability bar — the retention, CPI, and ROAS a growth round is underwritten on. That scorecard lives in Product OKRs — 2025 H1. Attribution across every title is standardised on Singular.

Where we are today: we've hit our tactical targets (ship dates, CPI), but day-30 retention and payback haven't yet cleared the bar a growth round is priced on. After the October 2025 cost reductions we're running on a lean core team while we pursue a bridge or strategic outcome to fund the next iteration. The near-term focus is proving day-30 retention holds — in hybrid-casual, the marketing-and-product seam only pays off if players stay past day one.

First-line playbook for the four player-facing issues that drive the bulk of our inbound. It lets anyone covering the queue triage, reply, and escalate consistently. Scope is the live titles: Domino Delights (internal codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes"), Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" in stores) and Combo Fighter. When a symptom matches a known incident, say so plainly and give a real ETA rather than a canned apology.

Always capture platform + store version + device model and, where the player can find it, their in-game user id (Settings → About → tap the build number). Most escalations stall because the ticket is missing one of these.

Triage table

Match the reported symptom to the row, apply the resolution, and only escalate if the resolution does not clear it.

SymptomLikely causeFirst-line resolutionEscalate to
Lives not regenerating / timer stuckJuly 2025 scheduler outage (event/lives loop stalled)Confirm the window; grant a lives top-up as goodwill; reassure that regeneration resumes once the scheduler is advancingBackend (Live-Ops scheduler)
Lost progression / account back at level 1June 2025 device-ID wipe (new device id, old save orphaned)Look up the old user id by email/receipt and re-link the current install (see below)Backend (account re-link)
Quests not appearing / empty slotsNov 2024 quest incident (population/reset regression)Force a session refresh; if slots stay empty, collect user id + timestamp and flagDesign + Backend (quests)
Frozen on splash at ~22%May 2025 font/asset download stallAsk them to switch networks (Wi-Fi ↔ cellular), clear app cache, and reinstall; confirm it reaches gameplayClient / QA

Account re-link (June 2025 wipe)

A device-ID change orphaned some saves, dropping players to a fresh level-1 account while their real progression still exists under the previous id. Do not tell them the data is gone.

  • Ask for the account email and, ideally, a store receipt or order id.
  • Look up the old user id in the support console by that email; confirm the level/coin balance matches their description.
  • File a re-link request to Backend with both ids so the current install points at the old save.

Never issue a compensating grant before a re-link — you would be topping up the empty new account, not the recovered one, and the balances double up after the merge. Grants come after the save is restored.

Canned responses

Personalise the greeting, keep the facts. Do not promise fixes we have not shipped.

  • Lives stuck: "We had a scheduler issue that paused life regeneration for some players; it's being addressed and your lives will resume filling automatically. I've added a top-up in the meantime."
  • Lost progress: "Your progression isn't lost — a device change created a new profile. Send me the email on the account and I'll re-link it to your original save."
  • Missing quests: "Quests should repopulate after a fresh session. If they're still empty, reply with your user id and when you noticed and I'll escalate."
  • Stuck at 22%: "That's a loading stall on our end. Please switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, clear the app cache, and reinstall."

Known-issue notes arrive from QA before a build ships — see the QA Regression Runbook — and symptoms found during a submission are mirrored here via the Release Checklist & Store Submission.

Owner: Vincent Parker (QA) · Space: OPS. This is the gate every Harmony Games title passes before we submit a build to the App Store or Google Play. It applies to Zombie Match 3D (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies"), Domino Delights (internal codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes") and Combo Fighter. Do not submit a build until every box below is ticked and QA has signed off — the checklist exists because every item on it maps to a real incident that shipped.

Always test the UPDATE path from the last two shipped versions (N-1 and N-2), not just a fresh install. The June 2025 progression wipe reproduced only when updating over a previously-shipped build; a clean install looked perfectly healthy. A fresh-install-only pass does not clear this gate.

Pre-submission checklist

Build & QA

  • Full manual regression is green on real iOS and Android hardware — see the QA Regression Runbook. QA sign-off is a hard gate.
  • Update path verified from N-1 and N-2: level, coins and unlocks survive the update; no save/progression loss.
  • Splash and loading screen watched all the way to gameplay on a throttled connection and with the app cache cleared — no stall (see incidents below).
  • Live quest config, if touched, has passed QA and a canary — nothing pushed straight to the live quest server (see the Quest System — Design & Incident Postmortem).

Store metadata & compliance

  • Version and build number bumped; release notes drafted for both stores.
  • Screenshots, age rating and data-safety / privacy declarations current.
  • IAP products and prices active in App Store Connect and Play Console before submission.
  • Analytics build tagged so installs attribute correctly (Singular).

Domino Delights is in maintenance mode — the current build is tracked under ENG-2366 (Jul 2025): IAP catalog refresh, difficulty tuning, interstitials disabled, and the lives regeneration fix. Run the same update-path and store checks against it; maintenance does not mean unreviewed.

Lessons from incidents

Each row is a bug that reached players. Treat the corresponding checklist item as non-negotiable.

TicketTitle / dateWhat happenedChecklist item it hardened
ENG-2346ZM3D global launch, May 15 2025Remote font/asset download made the game look frozen at ~22% on the splash screen. Fixed by changing when fonts load and adding a downloading indicator.Watch splash to gameplay on a slow connection with cache cleared.
ENG-2343ZM3D global launch, May 15 2025Splash / loading screen resolution issue at launch.Verify splash and loading render correctly across device resolutions.
—Progression wipe, June 2025Player progression wiped on update; reproduced on the update path only, not fresh install.Test update from N-1 and N-2; confirm save/progression integrity.
ENG-2366Domino Delights maintenance, Jul 2025Maintenance build: IAP refresh, difficulty tuning, interstitials disabled, lives fix.Run full store + update checks even on maintenance-mode builds.

When any check fails, block the release, file the bug with device / OS / source build, and do not ship until it is green.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 9, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0012", "created_at": "2024-07-01T17:26:08Z", "updated_at": "2025-07-26T08:50:17Z"}, {"id": "page_qa_runbook", "space_id": "space_ENG", "parent_id": "page_eng_home", "title": "QA Regression Runbook", "body": "

Manual QA regression pass run against every release candidate before we submit a build for review. Owned by QA (Vincent); anyone cutting a build can run it, but a green matrix here is a gate on the Release Checklist & Store Submission. Scope covers Domino Delights (internal codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes"), Zombie Match 3D (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies") and Combo Fighter. Keep it to ~45 minutes per title; if something fails, file the bug and block the release, don't hand-wave it.

Test the UPDATE path, not just a fresh install. The June 2025 ZM3D progression wipe only reproduced when updating from a previously-shipped version — a clean install looked perfectly healthy. Every candidate must be installed over the last two shipped versions and checked for save/progression loss before we ship. If we only test fresh installs we will miss this entire class of bug again.

Recurring bug classes to always check

These four have all bitten us in production. Treat them as non-negotiable checks on every pass, on real devices, not just the emulator.

  • Font / asset download stall on splash. In May 2025 ZM3D froze at roughly 22% on the splash screen while pulling remote fonts and assets. Watch the loading bar all the way to gameplay; test on a throttled/slow connection and with the app cache cleared.
  • Lives & scheduler regeneration. Confirm lives tick back up on the timer, refill correctly after device clock changes, and that offline time is credited without over-granting.
  • Quest population & reset. New quests populate on a fresh session, complete correctly, and roll over at the daily/weekly reset without duplicating or leaving empty slots.
  • Save / progression integrity. Level, coins and unlocks survive an update, a force-quit and a re-launch. This is the one the June 2025 wipe belongs to.

Regression matrix

Run each row on at least one iOS and one Android device. Both update rows are mandatory — N-1 and N-2 are the last two shipped store versions.

AreaFresh installUpdate from N-1Update from N-2Notes
Splash / asset loadPassPassPassWatch for the ~22% stall (May 2025 ZM3D)
Save / progressionPassPassPassJune 2025 wipe reproduced on update only
Lives & schedulerPassPassPassTest with device clock changes
Quests populate / resetPassPassPassCheck daily + weekly rollover
Purchase / restorePassPassPassSandbox account; confirm entitlements restore

If a check fails

  • File the bug with device, OS version, source build and repro steps, and link it here.
  • A failure in any UPDATE column blocks the release — fresh-install-only regressions do not pass the gate.
  • Player-facing symptoms (lost progress, stuck splash, missing lives) should be mirrored to the Customer Support Playbook so support has a known-issue note before it hits the store.

Once the matrix is green, tick the QA sign-off on the Release Checklist & Store Submission before submitting to the stores.

Per-title regression matrix

Each release candidate is walked through the full matrix below on at least one iOS and one Android device. A cell fails the gate if the observed behaviour deviates from the expected column; file the bug, mark the matrix red, and block the submission.

AreaCheckExpectedDominoZM3DCombo
First-time UXFresh install → tutorial → first winNo stall; tutorial completes; first level winnableYesYesYes
Font / localisationCold start on a fresh device (no cached font)UI renders; no blank/boxed glyphs at ~22% loadYesYesn/a
ProgressionPlay 3 levels, force-quit, relaunchLevel and currency persist; no reset to level 1YesYesYes
EconomyEarn + spend coins, buy a boosterBalances reconcile; booster consumed onceYesYesn/a
Live-opsEnter the active event; complete a questEvent loads; quest ticks; rewards grantedYesYesn/a
IAPSandbox purchase + restoreReceipt validated; entitlement restored on reinstallYesYesn/a
AdsWatch a rewarded ad to completionReward granted once; no double-grant on retryYesYesn/a

Known-issue regression cases

These are the incidents that have bitten us in production; every one now has a permanent regression case so it cannot silently return. Reproduce the trigger, confirm the fix holds.

Font-download stall. On a fresh device the dynamic font pack could fail to download, freezing the UI at ~22% of the tutorial. Regression: install on a wiped device with a throttled connection; confirm a fallback font renders and load continues.

Progression reset. A device-identifier change once wiped returning players back to level 1. Regression: migrate a save across a reinstall; confirm the cloud save rehydrates and no reset occurs.

Quest not resetting / not populating. A bad deploy left the daily quest board empty. Regression: roll the clock across a UTC day boundary; confirm quests repopulate and completion state resets.

Device lab

The minimum matrix is one recent + one old device per platform. We keep a small physical lab plus a cloud device farm for the long tail.

PlatformRecentOld / min-specTablet
iOScurrent-gen iPhone, latest OSiPhone SE-class, oldest supported OSiPad (one gen)
Androidcurrent-gen Samsung / Pixellow-RAM device, oldest supported OSone Android tablet

Sign-off

QA posts the completed matrix in #ops and links it from the release ticket. A build without a green matrix does not get submitted — no exceptions during the weekday release window, and never on a Friday.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 6, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0012", "created_at": "2024-04-15T10:11:23Z", "updated_at": "2025-07-01T12:48:13Z"}, {"id": "page_backend_services", "space_id": "space_ENG", "parent_id": "page_arch_overview", "title": "Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix", "body": "

This page describes the Elixir/Phoenix backend services that sit behind the Harmony Games clients — Domino Delights ("Game of Dominoes"/GoD internally), Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" in-store), and Combo Fighter. The services own authoritative game state, player profiles, quests, and live-ops delivery. For the wider system picture and how these tie into Unity and Nakama, see Architecture Overview; realtime multiplayer and matchmaking are documented separately in Nakama Server Setup & Operations.

Ownership is deliberately thin — a ~16-person studio can't staff a service mesh. One Elixir umbrella app, one Aurora cluster, a handful of Fargate tasks. Prefer boring and observable over clever.

Runtime & deployment

All services run as a single Elixir umbrella project, released with mix release and packaged into one container image. We run separate ECS Fargate services off that image (state, profile, quests, live-ops) so we can scale and roll them independently without maintaining separate codebases. Persistence is a shared Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with a schema per bounded context; the reader endpoint is used for analytics-adjacent queries so we don't contend with write traffic.

  • Compute: ECS Fargate, one task definition per service, behind an internal ALB.
  • Data: Aurora PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ), Ecto for access, migrations gated in CI.
  • Infra as code: everything provisioned via AWS CDK — VPC, clusters, task definitions, and Aurora are all defined in the CDK app so environments (staging/prod) stay in lockstep.

Auth

There is no third-party auth broker. A small custom identity service issues short-lived JWTs on login; every other service validates the JWT signature locally (no per-request network hop) and trusts the sub claim as the player ID. Device-bound refresh tokens are stored in the identity service's own schema. Live-ops and quest mutations additionally require an internal service token — never a player JWT.

Services

ServiceResponsibilityDatastore
identityLogin, JWT issuance/rotation, device bindingAurora (schema: identity)
game_stateAuthoritative match/board state, progression, save reconciliationAurora (schema: state)
profilePlayer profile, inventory, wallet (coins/lives)Aurora (schema: profile)
questsQuest definitions, assignment, and completion trackingAurora (schema: quests)
live_opsEvent scheduling, feature-flag delivery, seasonal contentAurora (schema: liveops)

Endpoints & releasing

Phoenix serves a thin JSON API — no HTML, no channels here (realtime lives in Nakama). Routes are versioned under /api/v1 and health-checked at /healthz for the ALB. A representative controller and the release command:

elixir id}) do case Profile.get_player(id) do {:ok, player} -> json(conn, %{id: player.id, coins: player.coins, lives: player.lives}) {:error, :not_found} -> conn |> put_status(:not_found) |> json(%{error: "not_found"}) end end end # Build + run the release (baked into the Fargate image) # MIX_ENV=prod mix release harmony_backend # _build/prod/rel/harmony_backend/bin/harmony_backend start]]>

Migrations do not run on boot. Run bin/harmony_backend eval "HarmonyBackend.Release.migrate()" as a one-off Fargate task before rolling the services, so a bad migration can't take down every task at once.

Owner: Douglas. Ping in #eng-backend before schema changes to the shared Aurora cluster — profile and game_state both read the wallet columns.

Combo Fighter is a merge / auto-battler prototype: the player drags Tetris-shaped pieces onto a board, merges matching pieces to upgrade them, connects them into combos, and then watches an auto-battle phase resolve the round. It was the last new concept Harmony Games took to a testable build — a skeleton crew put a playable MVP together in roughly four to five weeks (late 2025 into January 2026). Of the three prototypes we shipped to store test tracks it posted the strongest early engagement, but it remains parked: we haven't put UA spend behind it yet to see whether that engagement holds at scale.

Core Mechanics

A round has two distinct phases. The build phase is board manipulation; the battle phase is hands-off resolution.

Build phase

  • Drag & place. The tray offers Tetris-shaped pieces (I, L, S, T, square). The player drags a piece onto the board; it snaps to the grid.
  • Merge to upgrade. Two same-tier pieces of the same type that touch merge into the next tier — the familiar merge-2 loop, but on shaped pieces rather than single cells.
  • Connect for combos. Pieces wired into a contiguous chain form a combo; longer chains grant a battle-phase multiplier, so board layout drives power.

Battle phase

  • The assembled board becomes the player's squad and auto-battles the level's wave. No input during battle — the round is won or lost on how the board was built.
  • Rewards are gold only. Gold funds re-rolls and starting-piece upgrades. No gems, no energy, no second currency in the MVP.

Ads: None in MVP. There is no ad SDK, no interstitials, and no rewarded placements in the prototype. Monetization was deliberately deferred until the core loop proved it retained — the test builds measured engagement and retention only.

Art direction

Simple Chibi-style 3D characters on a clean board. The look was chosen to be cheap to produce at prototype scale while still reading as a finished game in a store screenshot.

Scope — MVP

The build track was a 35-level MVP carved out of a 163-level full design. The MVP existed to answer one question — does the merge-plus-auto-battle loop hold a player past the first session — before committing to the remaining content and the deeper progression curve.

  • Shipped in MVP: 35 levels, drag/merge/connect build loop, auto-battle resolution, gold economy, Chibi 3D art.
  • Designed but not built: levels 36–163, meta-progression between runs, monetization surface, live-ops events.

Builds & Early Retention

Three test builds went out over roughly two weeks in January and early February 2026. D1 retention climbed with each build even as install volume swung with test-track promotion.

BuildRelease dateInstallsD1 retention
1.0.62Jan 21, 202612725%
1.0.72Jan 25, 202624431%
1.0.88Feb 4, 20263043%

Session length was the standout signal: Combo Fighter averaged roughly 60 minutes of play on the day of install (D0) — the best of the three games we prototyped. By 1.0.88 the loop was tightening and D1 had reached 43% on a small install base, but we have not yet validated that at scale on a larger install base.

Related Pages

Prototype targets and the retention bar this work was measured against live in the H1 product objectives: Product OKRs — 2025 H1.

This page documents how gameplay telemetry flows from the Unity client into our analytics warehouse. It is the reference for anyone instrumenting a new event or writing a Snowflake query for a dashboard. For where this sits in the broader system, see Architecture Overview.

Scope: hybrid-casual titles across the studio — Domino Delights (codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes"), Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" on store), and Combo Fighter. All three share one instrumentation library and one pipeline.

Pipeline overview

The Unity client emits events through the Firebase Analytics SDK. From there a game-analytics pipeline streams events into AWS, transforms them, and lands them in object storage, from which the warehouse loads. The stages:

  • Unity client → Firebase — the client batches events and hands them to the Firebase Analytics SDK on-device.
  • Firebase → Kinesis — events are forwarded into an AWS Kinesis stream for ingestion.
  • Kinesis → Glue — an AWS Glue job validates and transforms records (flattens the event envelope, casts types, partitions by date).
  • Glue → S3 — both a raw/ and a processed/ prefix are written to S3.
  • S3 → Snowflake — the BI/warehouse layer loads from the S3 processed/ prefix. Analysts query Snowflake for dashboards and ad-hoc analysis.

Install attribution is handled separately by Singular (our MMP); attribution results are joined into Snowflake for UA reporting rather than flowing through the client event stream.

Event categories

Every event carries a common envelope (app version, platform, device class, session id, server timestamp). At a high level events fall into five categories:

CategoryFires onUsed for
SessionApp open / close, foreground / backgroundDAU, session length, retention curves
ProgressionLevel start / complete / failDifficulty tuning, funnel drop-off
Resource / economyCurrency and life grant / spendSink-source balance, economy health
Ad impressionRewarded / interstitial shown & completedAd revenue, fill rate, eCPM
Client errorHandled exceptions, load stallsCrash triage, release health

Load macro (Glue → S3 → Snowflake)

The warehouse pulls the Glue output from S3 with a scheduled COPY. Sketch of the load:

sql

The COPY is append-only and idempotent per partition — never TRUNCATE the landing table to "reload", or you drop history the marts depend on. Backfills replay a specific dt= partition only.

Adding or changing an event

  • Register the event name and payload in the shared instrumentation library before shipping — do not free-type event names in game code.
  • New fields must be nullable; the Glue transform tolerates extra keys but will not backfill missing ones.
  • Flag any type change (int → string, etc.) to eng before release — it breaks the Snowflake COPY column mapping.

This page describes the runtime architecture behind Harmony Games' live mobile titles — Domino Delights (internal codename Game of Dominoes / GoD) and Zombie Match 3D (store name Puzzles vs Zombies) — plus the shared platform that Combo Fighter and future titles ride on. It is the canonical starting point for new engineers; deep-dives live on the linked pages.

All of this runs in a single AWS account per environment (staging and prod). Infra is defined in AWS CDK (v2, TypeScript) — there is no click-ops. If it's not in the CDK app, it doesn't exist. See the AWS Infrastructure Guide for the account layout and deploy flow.

Client tier

Both live games ship a single Unity codebase built for iOS and Android. The Unity client is a fairly thin presentation layer: it renders the board, handles input and local animation, and caches recent state so a cold start feels instant. Authoritative game logic — economy, matchmaking, progression, anti-cheat validation — lives server-side. Clients talk to the backend over HTTPS/JSON and hold a short-lived session token issued at login.

  • Store builds are cut from Unity Cloud Build; release tagging is manual per title.
  • Attribution and install tracking go through Singular; there is no second attribution SDK in the client.
  • Telemetry is emitted from the client and does not hit the backend directly — see the analytics section below.

Backend services

Backend services are written in Elixir/Phoenix and run as containers on AWS ECS Fargate behind a single shared Application Load Balancer. Each service is its own task definition and target group, routed by host/path rule at the ALB. State is persisted in Aurora PostgreSQL (RDS, Multi-AZ in prod). We lean on Elixir's supervision trees and BEAM concurrency so a crashing session process never takes down the node. Details and the service catalog live on Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix.

Social & multiplayer

The social and real-time multiplayer layer is Nakama, run as its own Fargate service against a dedicated Aurora database. Nakama owns friends, leaderboards, chat, and the authoritative match runtime for head-to-head modes in Combo Fighter and GoD. Our Phoenix services call Nakama over its internal API rather than reimplementing sessions or presence. Operational runbooks are on Nakama Server Setup & Operations.

Component summary

ComponentTechRuns onNotes
Game clientUnity (C#)iOS / AndroidThin client; one codebase per title
Game backendElixir / PhoenixECS Fargate + ALBAuthoritative economy & progression
Social / multiplayerNakamaECS FargateFriends, leaderboards, chat, matches
Primary datastoreAurora PostgreSQLRDS (Multi-AZ)Separate cluster per service group
Infra as codeAWS CDK v2CISingle account per environment

Telemetry & analytics

Gameplay and monetization events flow from the Unity client into Firebase, are streamed into AWS Kinesis, transformed by AWS Glue, and landed in S3 for the warehouse. The backend is deliberately out of this path so a telemetry spike never adds load to the game services. The full pipeline, schemas, and dashboards are documented on Analytics Integration — Unity → Snowflake.

Keep this page conceptual. Do not paste account IDs, ALB DNS names, connection strings, or bundle IDs here — those belong in the AWS Infrastructure Guide and the secrets manager, not the wiki.

Welcome to Harmony Games, Inc. (harmonygames.co). This is the studio overview for new hires — who we are, what we're building, and how we work. Read it first, then jump to the space for your discipline.

Who we are

Harmony Games is a small, remote-first mobile-game studio, founded in March 2023 and incorporated the following month in Delaware. We build hybrid-casual puzzle games — titles with the instant approachability of a casual game and the retention hooks of a light RPG. The team is distributed across three continents and runs lean by design (around sixteen people at its peak), keeping everyone close to the product.

The founding thesis comes from a specific background: 10+ years in gaming marketing plus a psychology degree. That pairing is the whole company in one sentence — we sit on the seam between marketing and product, and build games where the acquisition funnel and the core loop are designed together rather than handed off.

Mission

“A game of dominoes is really just match-3 in disguise — the same metrics, the same funnel. The opportunity is to take that casual approachability and deepen it: collection mechanics and a light RPG economy that give a player a reason to come back on day 30. Bridge marketing and product, and you get a game that is both cheap to acquire for and worth staying in.”

What we're building

Our titles, in the order the studio's focus moved to each:

WhenTitleDetail
Mar–Apr 2023Founded & incorporatedHarmony Games, Inc. founded March 2023; Delaware incorporation April 2023.
2023–2024Domino DelightsFirst title (internal codename "Game of Dominoes" / GoD) — tile-match with collection meta; benchmarked against Domino Dreams.
Jan 2025Zombie Match 3DStudio focus shifts to the match-3D RPG (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies"), benchmarked against Match Factory.
2025Combo Fighter (prototype)A third concept taken to prototype to test whether the hybrid-casual formula generalises beyond tile-match.

How we measure success

We measure product ambition against a fundability bar — the retention, CPI, and ROAS a growth round is underwritten on. That scorecard lives in Product OKRs — 2025 H1. Attribution across every title is standardised on Singular.

Where we are today: we've hit our tactical targets (ship dates, CPI), but day-30 retention and payback haven't yet cleared the bar a growth round is priced on. After the October 2025 cost reductions we're running on a lean core team while we pursue a bridge or strategic outcome to fund the next iteration. The near-term focus is proving day-30 retention holds — in hybrid-casual, the marketing-and-product seam only pays off if players stay past day one.

This page documents how Harmony Games runs its backend on AWS. It complements the Architecture Overview (the big picture) and the Nakama Server Setup & Operations runbook (the game-server specifics). If you are new to the infra, read the Architecture Overview first, then come back here for the AWS-level detail.

We are a ~16-person studio, so the guiding principle is managed over self-hosted. Almost everything below is a managed AWS service so we don't run a platform team. We bootstrapped the first two years largely on AWS Activate credits before we were paying list price.

Account & region layout

We run a single production AWS account (id 402118665390) plus a separate staging account (id 918273645012). Primary region is us-west-2; we keep a warm secondary footprint in us-east-2 for the analytics tier and disaster-recovery snapshots. Everything sits inside a multi-AZ VPC (three availability zones), with public subnets for the load balancer and private subnets for compute and data.

Services in use

LayerAWS serviceWhat it does for us
ComputeECS FargateRuns the containerized Phoenix API and the Nakama game server. No EC2 hosts to patch.
DatabaseAurora PostgreSQLPrimary transactional store for player state, economy and live-ops config. Multi-AZ writer + reader.
IngressApplication Load BalancerFronts the Fargate services; path-based routing to Phoenix vs Nakama.
CertificatesACMTLS certs for *.harmonygames.co, auto-renewed and attached to the ALB.
Event lakeS3Raw client and server events land here as the analytics data lake.
Streaming / ETLKinesis + GlueKinesis ingests the event firehose; Glue jobs transform and partition it before it feeds Snowflake.
ObservabilityCloudWatch + X-RayContainer logs, alarms and dashboards (CloudWatch) plus distributed traces across Phoenix and Nakama (X-Ray).

Analytics pipeline

The event path is worth calling out because it spans two regions. Clients and the game server emit events; those are written into Kinesis streams, dropped to S3 in raw form, and then Glue crawls and ETLs them into the curated tables our warehouse reads. This is the AWS half of the flow; the warehouse side lives on the analytics team's docs.

  • us-west-2 — game backend, Aurora, live ingestion.
  • us-east-2 — Glue jobs, curated S3, cross-region backup copies.

Deploys

Service images are built in CI and pushed to ECR, then rolled out to the relevant Fargate service with a rolling update behind the ALB health checks. There is no manual SSH step — a failed health check rolls the task back automatically.

Cost note (estimates only). These are rough monthly figures pulled from Cost Explorer for planning; treat them as directional, not billing-accurate.

  • Fargate (Phoenix + Nakama): ~$650/mo
  • Aurora PostgreSQL (writer + one reader): ~$420/mo
  • S3 + Kinesis + Glue (analytics): ~$300/mo
  • ALB + data transfer + CloudWatch/X-Ray: ~$180/mo

The single biggest lever is right-sizing Fargate task memory — check the CloudWatch utilization dashboard before bumping a task definition.

Ownership

Infra is owned by Douglas with backup from the platform on-call rotation. If you need a new IAM role, a subnet change, or a new Glue job, open an ENG ticket and tag it infra — do not click around in the console for anything that touches production networking.

Service inventory

Everything runs in the production account above, primary region us-west-2 (defined in the CDK app). Compute is containerised on ECS Fargate; state is Aurora PostgreSQL; the analytics path is Kinesis → Glue → S3.

ServiceAWS primitiveNotes
Game APIECS FargateElixir/Phoenix; autoscaled on CPU + request count behind an ALB
Social / accountsECS Fargate (Nakama)gRPC 7350 / HTTP 7351; Aurora-backed
Primary datastoreAurora PostgreSQLMulti-AZ writer + reader; automated snapshots
Event streamKinesis Data StreamsClient telemetry ingestion; feeds Glue
ETLAWS GlueBatches Kinesis records to partitioned Parquet in S3
LakeS3Partitioned by event date; the BI warehouse loads from here

Scaling & limits

Fargate services scale horizontally; Aurora scales the reader fleet for read-heavy analytics-adjacent queries. Peak concurrency tracked ~6–7K DAU, so headroom is generous and cost, not capacity, is the constraint.

Cost control: non-prod environments scale to zero overnight; Kinesis shard count is reviewed monthly against throttling metrics. The AWS activation credits materially offset the first year of spend.

Deploy & rollback

Infrastructure is AWS CDK; application deploys are rolling on Fargate with health-check gating. Rollback is redeploy of the previous task-definition revision.

Disaster recovery

Aurora automated backups + manual pre-release snapshots; S3 is versioned and the lake is reproducible from Kinesis replay within the retention window. RPO is the snapshot cadence; RTO is dominated by Aurora restore time.

FailureMitigationRecovery
Writer AZ lossMulti-AZ AuroraAutomatic failover to standby
Bad migrationPre-release snapshotRestore snapshot; replay Kinesis
Accidental S3 deleteBucket versioningRestore prior version

On-call

Alarms page the two-person rota via the on-call tool. The first responder triages; anything touching Aurora or a data migration escalates to Arthur before any write action.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 6, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0031", "created_at": "2023-07-15T10:36:50Z", "updated_at": "2025-08-01T10:29:36Z"}, {"id": "page_live_ops_engine", "space_id": "space_ENG", "parent_id": "page_eng_home", "title": "Live-Ops Event Engine", "body": "

The Live-Ops Event Engine powers all recurring in-game events for Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" in stores). It defines, schedules, and fires timed content — Plague Race, Zombie Lane, Endless Monster Mode — and drives the associated leaderboards and lives economy. This page documents the architecture, the scheduler's known fragility, and the July 2025 outage that materially hit revenue. For upcoming cadence and slot ownership see Live-Ops Event Calendar & Planning.

Architecture

The engine has three cooperating parts. Event definitions are static config authored by design; the scheduler is the runtime that evaluates windows and fires state transitions; the leaderboard service ranks entries and settles rewards at event close.

ComponentResponsibilityOwner
Event definitionsDeclarative config: event type, reward table, start/end windows, cohort targetingDesign (Julia)
SchedulerTicks every 60s; opens/closes events and regenerates player lives on the same loopBackend (Douglas)
Leaderboard serviceIngests scores during a window, freezes and settles rewards at closeBackend

The lives coupling

A deliberate but risky decision: player life regeneration runs on the same scheduler tick loop as event firing. This keeps the timing model simple, but it means one failure mode takes down two player-facing systems at once. See the incident below.

Scheduler is a single point of failure. There is one active scheduler process with no hot standby. If it stalls, live events stop firing and lives stop regenerating. Do not add new subsystems to the tick loop without a leader-election plan.

July 2025 outage

Between roughly Jul 12–26, 2025, the event/lives scheduler stopped advancing. The first player-visible symptom was lives no longer regenerating, first observed around 03:41 on Jul 13, 2025. No scheduled live events fired for the duration of the window, and store revenue dipped materially — on the order of 30% across the outage — as the core reason-to-return loop went dark. No standalone ticket was cut at the time; the timeline was reconstructed after the fact from warehouse metrics and scheduler logs.

The 30% revenue figure is coherence-locked to the BI warehouse. Treat the warehouse aggregation as the source of truth for the outage window; do not re-derive it from raw event logs, which are incomplete for those days.

Remediation

  • Add a heartbeat + external watchdog that pages on a missed scheduler tick (target: alert within 5 minutes, not 12+ hours).
  • Decouple life regeneration from event firing so a scheduler stall degrades one system, not both.
  • Introduce leader election so a second process can take over the tick loop.
  • Backfill a lives-regeneration reconciler that can catch a cohort up after a stall.
  • Dashboard the scheduler's last-tick timestamp alongside revenue so drift is visible on the same screen.

Design context for the coupled lives/event model and the related quest timing regression lives in Quest System — Design & Incident Postmortem.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 8, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0031", "created_at": "2024-08-15T16:07:58Z", "updated_at": "2025-08-01T08:11:12Z"}, {"id": "page_zm3d_gdd", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_prod_home", "title": "Zombie Match 3D — Game Design Document", "body": "

This is the living Game Design Document for Zombie Match 3D (store title Puzzles vs Zombies). It is the source of truth for the core loop, the RPG combat layer, and monetization. For the coin/life economy see Economy Design — Coins, Lives & Boosters, and for the paid track see ZM3D Season Pass — Spec. This document ladders up to Product OKRs — 2025 H1.

Global launch shipped May 15, 2025. This GDD reflects the launch build plus the Season Pass update.

Core mechanic

The matcher is a Match-3D collector benchmarked on Match Factory. Objects sit in a physics pile; the player drags items into a 7-slot tray. Collect any 3 matching objects and they clear from the tray. If all 7 slots fill without a match, the board is lost. Tray pressure is the primary difficulty dial.

  • Pile physics — objects settle and occlude each other; digging exposes buried matches.
  • 7-slot tray — the fail state; tuning slot count changes felt difficulty more than object count.
  • Object families — cosmetic skins that map to elemental ammo in the RPG layer.

Zombie RPG layer

Levels wrap the matcher in combat. Each cleared triple fires the matching element at the current monster. Monsters carry an elemental weakness; hitting the weakness deals bonus damage and can apply a status.

Monster / element table

Monster archetypeWeaknessOn-hit effect
Sparkbound WalkershockChain damage to adjacent enemies
Bloated CarrierpoisonDamage-over-time stack
Charred HuskburnArmor melt
Frostbitten CrawlerfreezeSkips next attack
Bog LurkersplashArea splash to the pack
RioterstunInterrupt current wind-up
Slick RunnerglueMovement pinned
ScreecherblindAttack accuracy drop

Modes

  • Campaign — authored levels, escalating monster mixes.
  • Endless — survival board with an item refill every 30s to keep the pile stocked.
  • Infinite-HP Boss — a damage-race against a boss whose HP does not deplete to zero; the score is total damage dealt before the tray fills.

Monetization

The headline product is the Season Pass at $6.99, launched Jul 15, 2025. It runs a free and a premium reward track over a fixed season window; progression is earned through campaign and Endless play. Coin, life, and booster sinks live in the linked Economy doc — do not duplicate values here.

Known launch issues (tracked, historical):

  • Hard crash tied to a potion / addressables load path (May 2025) on some devices during first combat.
  • Font-download freeze that stalls the splash screen at ~22% on slow connections.

Boss mode reward config

Owner: Robert (Product). Design: Julia Lawson. Changes to tray count or refill cadence must be reviewed against the OKR dashboard before shipping.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 11, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0016", "created_at": "2025-01-20T09:00:52Z", "updated_at": "2025-07-15T11:58:41Z"}, {"id": "page_domino_gdd", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_prod_home", "title": "Domino Delights — Game Design Document", "body": "

Domino Delights (internal codename "Game of Dominoes" / GoD) is Harmony Games' tile-connecting puzzle title with light-RPG progression. This document is the living design reference for the core loop, character system, and retention mini-games. Store title is Domino Delights; use Game of Dominoes or GoD internally.

Soft-launched under the Baklava release (~Aug 2024). ~4,000 levels are in production. This GDD supersedes the pre-soft-launch draft; see the version history for the edit trail.

Core Loop & Mechanics

Players connect and match adjacent dominoes on a board to clear level objectives. Each cleared cluster feeds a combo meter; sustained combos drive the light-RPG layer, where collected characters level up and unlock stronger board-clearing abilities. A single run alternates between board-clearing turns and character-ability triggers, keeping session length short but replayable across the ~4,000-level ladder.

Boosts

  • Magical Gust — a wind boost that clears all face-up tiles on the board, resetting a stalled position.
  • Character abilities (below) act as targeted boosts that recharge through matching.

For coin, life, and booster balancing that these mechanics feed into, see Economy Design — Coins, Lives & Boosters.

Characters

Five collectible characters, each with its own upgrade track. Leveling a character deepens its signature effect and reduces its recharge cost.

CharacterSignature abilityUpgrade track
SophieDrops massive tiles that clear a wide area on contactIncreases tile size and blast radius
NathanRemoves a set of random tiles from the boardIncreases tiles removed per trigger
JuliusChains matches across the board for a combo bonusExtends chain length and combo multiplier
WildcardAdapts to the current objective, filling in the scarcest tile typeImproves match accuracy and recharge speed
Fifth (TBD)Reserved slot for the next collection waveDesign pending post-soft-launch data

Character names and the fifth slot are provisional. Do not surface upgrade numbers in marketing until the economy pass locks recharge costs.

Retention Mini-Games

Between level runs, players can enter reward mini-games that keep engagement high on off-days:

  • Tile Dozer — a coin-pusher where dropped tiles shove a stacked tray toward the edge for coin and booster payouts.
  • Plinko — a drop-and-bounce board awarding tiered rewards by landing slot.
  • Conveyor Belt — a timed grab mini-game where players pull prizes off a moving belt.

Reward scaling for Tile Dozer and the other mini-games is tuned to daily-return targets and shares the coin sink with the core economy.

Competitive Context

Positioning benchmarks against the tile-matching leader are tracked in Competitive Analysis — Match Factory.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 12, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0016", "created_at": "2023-06-01T09:12:58Z", "updated_at": "2025-07-15T10:04:41Z"}, {"id": "page_season_pass_spec", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_zm3d_gdd", "title": "ZM3D Season Pass — Spec", "body": "

This is the product spec for the Zombie Match 3D Season Pass (store title Puzzles vs Zombies), written just before launch. The pass is the first recurring paid product on the title and the primary lever we have for lifting ARPU on our existing daily actives. For the core loop, combat layer, and monetization overview this ladders under, see Zombie Match 3D — Game Design Document, and for the target it serves see Product OKRs — 2025 H1.

At a glance. Launches Jul 15, 2025 at $6.99/month. A free track and a premium track run in parallel over a monthly season window, with rewards unlocked by the same live-ops progression players already earn through play.

Goal & positioning

We monetize almost entirely through consumables (coins, boosters, extra lives). That caps ARPU because it only reaches players already willing to spend on a fail state. The Season Pass adds a low-friction, predictable monthly product that converts engagement — not frustration — into revenue, and gives non-payers a visible reason to log in daily via the free track.

  • Cadence — one season per calendar month; the track resets and re-themes on the 1st.
  • Earn, don't grind — pass points come from campaign clears, Endless runs, and daily quests. No separate currency to buy.
  • Free track always on — every player earns from tier 1; the premium track retro-unlocks all already-earned premium rewards at purchase.
  • One SKU — a single monthly unlock at $6.99. No tier-skips or per-level buys at launch; revisit after we read week-one conversion.

Reward tracks

Each season runs 30 tiers. The free track is deliberately front-loaded so the value of the premium track is legible before a player commits. Premium leans into cosmetics and the coin/gem sinks documented in the economy layer — it does not sell raw power.

Tier bandFree trackPremium track ($6.99)
1–5Coins, 1 boosterSeason avatar frame + coins
6–10Extra livesExclusive monster skin
11–20CoinsBooster bundles + gems
21–291 boosterCoins, gems, tray cosmetic
30Coin lump sumSignature seasonal skin + gem grant

Points model

Rollout

Ship to 100% on launch day rather than a slow ramp — the pass is time-boxed to the month, so a partial rollout would leave early cohorts on a shortened first season. We gate on store approval and a live-ops config freeze the day before.

Rollout guardrails:

  • Do not touch tray count or Endless refill cadence during an active season — it swings the difficulty curve and skews pass-progression pacing right when we're reading purchase intent.
  • Season config (tiers, rewards, theme) is authored in the live-ops tool and locked 24h before the 1st; no hotfixes to reward tables mid-season without Product sign-off.
  • Purchase, tier-claim, and daily-active events are tagged for reporting through our attribution and analytics stack so we can read conversion and IAP mix from day one.

By late summer the Season Pass had grown into a meaningful share of monthly IAP on Zombie Match 3D — enough that season pacing now factors into every difficulty and live-ops decision on the title. Owner: Robert (Product). Design partner: Julia Lawson.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 3, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0016", "created_at": "2025-06-20T11:51:04Z", "updated_at": "2025-07-14T13:37:05Z"}, {"id": "page_qa_runbook", "space_id": "space_ENG", "parent_id": "page_eng_home", "title": "QA Regression Runbook", "body": "

Manual QA regression pass run against every release candidate before we submit a build for review. Owned by QA (Vincent); anyone cutting a build can run it, but a green matrix here is a gate on the Release Checklist & Store Submission. Scope covers Domino Delights (internal codename GoD, "Game of Dominoes"), Zombie Match 3D (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies") and Combo Fighter. Keep it to ~45 minutes per title; if something fails, file the bug and block the release, don't hand-wave it.

Test the UPDATE path, not just a fresh install. The June 2025 ZM3D progression wipe only reproduced when updating from a previously-shipped version — a clean install looked perfectly healthy. Every candidate must be installed over the last two shipped versions and checked for save/progression loss before we ship. If we only test fresh installs we will miss this entire class of bug again.

Recurring bug classes to always check

These four have all bitten us in production. Treat them as non-negotiable checks on every pass, on real devices, not just the emulator.

  • Font / asset download stall on splash. In May 2025 ZM3D froze at roughly 22% on the splash screen while pulling remote fonts and assets. Watch the loading bar all the way to gameplay; test on a throttled/slow connection and with the app cache cleared.
  • Lives & scheduler regeneration. Confirm lives tick back up on the timer, refill correctly after device clock changes, and that offline time is credited without over-granting.
  • Quest population & reset. New quests populate on a fresh session, complete correctly, and roll over at the daily/weekly reset without duplicating or leaving empty slots.
  • Save / progression integrity. Level, coins and unlocks survive an update, a force-quit and a re-launch. This is the one the June 2025 wipe belongs to.

Regression matrix

Run each row on at least one iOS and one Android device. Both update rows are mandatory — N-1 and N-2 are the last two shipped store versions.

AreaFresh installUpdate from N-1Update from N-2Notes
Splash / asset loadPassPassPassWatch for the ~22% stall (May 2025 ZM3D)
Save / progressionPassPassPassJune 2025 wipe reproduced on update only
Lives & schedulerPassPassPassTest with device clock changes
Quests populate / resetPassPassPassCheck daily + weekly rollover
Purchase / restorePassPassPassSandbox account; confirm entitlements restore

If a check fails

  • File the bug with device, OS version, source build and repro steps, and link it here.
  • A failure in any UPDATE column blocks the release — fresh-install-only regressions do not pass the gate.
  • Player-facing symptoms (lost progress, stuck splash, missing lives) should be mirrored to the Customer Support Playbook so support has a known-issue note before it hits the store.

Once the matrix is green, tick the QA sign-off on the Release Checklist & Store Submission before submitting to the stores.

Per-title regression matrix

Each release candidate is walked through the full matrix below on at least one iOS and one Android device. A cell fails the gate if the observed behaviour deviates from the expected column; file the bug, mark the matrix red, and block the submission.

AreaCheckExpectedDominoZM3DCombo
First-time UXFresh install → tutorial → first winNo stall; tutorial completes; first level winnableYesYesYes
Font / localisationCold start on a fresh device (no cached font)UI renders; no blank/boxed glyphs at ~22% loadYesYesn/a
ProgressionPlay 3 levels, force-quit, relaunchLevel and currency persist; no reset to level 1YesYesYes
EconomyEarn + spend coins, buy a boosterBalances reconcile; booster consumed onceYesYesn/a
Live-opsEnter the active event; complete a questEvent loads; quest ticks; rewards grantedYesYesn/a
IAPSandbox purchase + restoreReceipt validated; entitlement restored on reinstallYesYesn/a
AdsWatch a rewarded ad to completionReward granted once; no double-grant on retryYesYesn/a

Known-issue regression cases

These are the incidents that have bitten us in production; every one now has a permanent regression case so it cannot silently return. Reproduce the trigger, confirm the fix holds.

Font-download stall. On a fresh device the dynamic font pack could fail to download, freezing the UI at ~22% of the tutorial. Regression: install on a wiped device with a throttled connection; confirm a fallback font renders and load continues.

Progression reset. A device-identifier change once wiped returning players back to level 1. Regression: migrate a save across a reinstall; confirm the cloud save rehydrates and no reset occurs.

Quest not resetting / not populating. A bad deploy left the daily quest board empty. Regression: roll the clock across a UTC day boundary; confirm quests repopulate and completion state resets.

Device lab

The minimum matrix is one recent + one old device per platform. We keep a small physical lab plus a cloud device farm for the long tail.

PlatformRecentOld / min-specTablet
iOScurrent-gen iPhone, latest OSiPhone SE-class, oldest supported OSiPad (one gen)
Androidcurrent-gen Samsung / Pixellow-RAM device, oldest supported OSone Android tablet

Sign-off

QA posts the completed matrix in #ops and links it from the release ticket. A build without a green matrix does not get submitted — no exceptions during the weekday release window, and never on a Friday.

This page is the cross-game reference for how our soft and hard currencies, lives, and boosters are priced and tuned. It is owned by Design and kept in sync with the individual game design docs — see Domino Delights — Game Design Document and Zombie Match 3D — Game Design Document for the per-game economy layers built on top of these primitives.

Currency model

Every title uses the same two-tier currency so tuning intuition transfers between games. Coins are the soft currency earned in play; gems are the premium hard currency bought or awarded sparingly. The conversion is fixed across the studio:

UnitEqualsNotes
1 US dollar1,000 coinsReference peg for IAP sizing; not a direct store SKU.
1 gem10 coinsHard currency; used for premium sinks and gating.

Level victories pay out roughly 40 gold on average, which anchors the earn side of the loop against the booster sinks below.

Zombie Match 3D item catalog

The ZM3D Master Item List is the source of truth for tunable objects: it currently holds 251 items spread across 23 categories (boosters, tiles, cosmetics, packs, and event-only entitlements). When adding a category, register it here first so the balancing sheet and the client stay aligned.

Booster costs

Boosters are the primary coin sink. Costs are deliberately clustered so players learn the price bands quickly rather than memorizing each item.

BoosterCoin cost
Catapult333
Broom333
Tornado333
Taser333
Glue300
Trampoline200
Super Broom500
  • The four core boosters share the 333 price point so they read as interchangeable power tools.
  • Trampoline is the cheap entry sink at 200 coins to seed early spending habits.
  • Super Broom sits at 500 as the premium clear; it is the main gem-to-coin bridge.

The Domino Delights coin cut (April 2025)

In April 2025 we cut Domino Delights coin rewards by roughly 50% to stop runaway coin inflation. The 99th-percentile daily earn fell from about 25,000 coins to about 9,000 coins. Do not revert reward payouts on GoD without re-running the sink analysis — the pre-cut curve was unrecoverable.

The symptom was that high-engagement players accumulated coins faster than any sink could absorb, so boosters felt free and the difficulty curve flattened. After the cut, average booster spend nudged up as expected and the coin balance distribution stopped climbing. The changes were applied to the live economy tables under the "Game of Dominoes" (GoD) codename and mirrored into this page's tuning constants.

Lives regeneration and refill pricing are game-specific and documented in each GDD. This page only fixes the shared currency and booster primitives.

", "body_format": "storage", "status": "current", "version": 9, "author_id": "user_EMPLOYEE_0005", "created_at": "2024-06-01T18:11:38Z", "updated_at": "2025-04-20T09:28:10Z"}, {"id": "page_competitive_analysis", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_prod_home", "title": "Competitive Analysis — Match Factory", "body": "

Working notes from the Jan 7, 2025 Prototype Discussion. We are deciding whether to keep iterating on Domino Delights (internal codename "Game of Dominoes" / GoD) or pivot the next title to a 3D physics-matcher. The reference the room kept returning to is Match Factory, the current gold standard for 3D matching. This page lays out why its core loop out-retains the domino approach, and how Zombie Match 3D (store name "Puzzles vs Zombies") adapts the mechanic without cloning it.

Comparisons to Match Factory and Domino Dreams are based on public store listings and hands-on play only. We have no first-party numbers for either; treat all competitor reads as directional.

Why Match Factory wins on retention

The Match Factory loop is deceptively simple: tap identical objects from a physics pile, and any three of a kind clear. The tension lives entirely in the 7-slot tray at the bottom. If all seven slots fill without completing a triplet, you lose the board. That one constraint does a lot of work:

  • Legible failure state. Players know exactly why they lost — the tray filled — so a retry feels earned.
  • Short sessions. A board resolves in under a minute, which suits commute play and drives strong D1.
  • Readable difficulty. Tune tension via pile variety against the fixed 7-slot capacity.

Our Domino Delights prototype (see Domino Delights — Game Design Document) never produced that pressure. Domino placement is open-ended, so there is no always-visible fail meter; sessions run long and the loss condition reads as fuzzy. Domino Dreams shows the same ceiling — pleasant, but softer hooks than the tray-based matchers.

Head-to-head

DimensionMatch Factory (3D matcher)Domino Delights / Domino Dreams
Core actionMatch 3 objects from a physics pilePlace and chain dominoes
Fail conditionFill the 7-slot tray, no tripletRun out of moves / soft block
Session lengthUnder a minute per boardMulti-minute, open-ended
Early retention readStrong D1, clean retry loopSofter hooks, fuzzier loss

How Zombie Match 3D differentiates

Cloning the loop is not the plan. Zombie Match 3D keeps the proven 7-slot tray as its puzzle skeleton, then stacks a zombie-combat RPG layer on top so matching drives more than clearing a board. Completed triplets resolve as attacks against a wave of zombies, turning each cleared set into combat output.

  • Puzzle skeleton (borrowed). Same physics pile and 7-slot fill-to-lose pressure players already understand from titles like Match Factory.
  • Combat layer (ours). Object types map to attack effects; the tray becomes a resource, not a pure meter.
  • RPG progression (ours). Upgrades and run structure give us a long-tail retention and monetization story the flat matcher category lacks.

Full mechanics and economy live in Zombie Match 3D — Game Design Document. The bet: inherit the matcher's clean, high-retention core and differentiate on combat/RPG, rather than competing head-on with an established pure-matcher.

Open question for the team: is the 7-slot constraint defensible design language rather than a copy? Consensus in the room was that pairing it with zombie combat clears that bar. — Robert

[{"id": "page_combo_gdd", "space_id": "space_PROD", "parent_id": "page_prod_home", "title": "Combo Fighter \u2014 Game Design Document", "body": "

Combo Fighter is a merge / auto-battler prototype: the player drags Tetris-shaped pieces onto a board, merges matching pieces to upgrade them, connects them into combos, and then watches an auto-battle phase resolve the round. It was the last new concept Harmony Games took to a testable build \u2014 a skeleton crew put a playable MVP together in roughly four to five weeks (late 2025 into January 2026). Of the three prototypes we shipped to store test tracks it posted the strongest early engagement, but it remains parked: we haven't put UA spend behind it yet to see whether that engagement holds at scale.

Core Mechanics

A round has two distinct phases. The build phase is board manipulation; the battle phase is hands-off resolution.

Build phase

  • Drag & place. The tray offers Tetris-shaped pieces (I, L, S, T, square). The player drags a piece onto the board; it snaps to the grid.
  • Merge to upgrade. Two same-tier pieces of the same type that touch merge into the next tier \u2014 the familiar merge-2 loop, but on shaped pieces rather than single cells.
  • Connect for combos. Pieces wired into a contiguous chain form a combo; longer chains grant a battle-phase multiplier, so board layout drives power.

Battle phase

  • The assembled board becomes the player's squad and auto-battles the level's wave. No input during battle \u2014 the round is won or lost on how the board was built.
  • Rewards are gold only. Gold funds re-rolls and starting-piece upgrades. No gems, no energy, no second currency in the MVP.

Ads: None in MVP. There is no ad SDK, no interstitials, and no rewarded placements in the prototype. Monetization was deliberately deferred until the core loop proved it retained \u2014 the test builds measured engagement and retention only.

Art direction

Simple Chibi-style 3D characters on a clean board. The look was chosen to be cheap to produce at prototype scale while still reading as a finished game in a store screenshot.

Scope \u2014 MVP

The build track was a 35-level MVP carved out of a 163-level full design. The MVP existed to answer one question \u2014 does the merge-plus-auto-battle loop hold a player past the first session \u2014 before committing to the remaining content and the deeper progression curve.

  • Shipped in MVP: 35 levels, drag/merge/connect build loop, auto-battle resolution, gold economy, Chibi 3D art.
  • Designed but not built: levels 36\u2013163, meta-progression between runs, monetization surface, live-ops events.

Builds & Early Retention

Three test builds went out over roughly two weeks in January and early February 2026. D1 retention climbed with each build even as install volume swung with test-track promotion.

BuildRelease dateInstallsD1 retention
1.0.62Jan 21, 202612725%
1.0.72Jan 25, 202624431%
